questions.question: What does the Arabic word 'tariq' literally mean, and how did the Makkan audience understand an oath sworn by it?
options: A. A thunderbolt; they understood it as a warning of immediate punishment
B. A traveler arriving after dark who knocks on a door; they recognized it as the most serious kind of oath
C. A shooting star used to ward off evil spirits; they saw it purely as a protective sign
D. The morning star; they understood it as a promise of a new beginning
questions.explanation: The layer 1 tafsir explains that 'tariq' comes from a root meaning to knock or strike and classically referred to a traveler who arrives after dark. The Makkan audience recognized that swearing by something majestic and beyond human control signaled the most serious of statements, commanding their full attention before the surah's momentous disclosure.

questions.question: True or false: verse 4 of Surah At-Tariq teaches that only believers have a guardian over them, while disbelievers are left without divine oversight.
questions.explanation: The layer 1 tafsir emphasizes the categorical Arabic construction 'in kullu nafsin' — 'there is not a single soul' — as affirming universality without any exception. Every human being, regardless of belief or status, has an appointed guardian (hafidh) over them who both protects and records.

questions.question: The command 'So let man observe from what he was created' (verse 5) addresses human arrogance by directing attention toward what?
options: A. The vastness of the universe and humanity's smallness within it
B. The humble, uncontrolled origins of every human life as a logical refutation of denying resurrection
C. The social inequalities produced by tribal pride in Makkan society
D. The miracles performed by previous prophets as evidence for divine power
questions.explanation: The layer 1 commentary explains that 'fal-yandur' is an imperative directing humanity to reflect on their own origins. As the tafsir states, no person chose to exist or designed their own creation — they arrived entirely dependent on divine will — making any pride before the Creator logically untenable and denial of resurrection irrational.

questions.question: True or false: the phrase 'qawl fasl' in verse 13 describes the Quran as a decisive, separating word that distinguishes truth from falsehood, directly rebutting the Makkan accusation that it was poetry or sorcery.
questions.explanation: The layer 1 tafsir of verse 13 explains that 'qawl fasl' combines 'qawl' (speech) with 'fasl' (decisive separation, clear judgment). Ibn Abbas interpreted 'fasl' as meaning 'true and real,' and Qatadah as 'a just and decisive ruling.' The verse categorically rejects the Makkan characterization of the Prophet's recitation as entertainment or trickery.

questions.question: Which Companions proposed specific identifications for 'al-najm al-thaqib,' and what was Imam al-Tabari's preferred interpretive position?
options: A. Ibn Umar and Ali identified it as the moon; Tabari accepted only this view
B. Ibn Abbas and Mujahid proposed identifications such as the Pleiades or Saturn; Tabari leaned toward the general reading that all stars qualify as 'thaqib'
C. Qatadah and al-Hasan al-Basri identified it exclusively as a comet; Tabari fully agreed
D. Abu Hurairah identified it as Jupiter; Tabari endorsed this as the sole sound opinion
questions.explanation: The layer 2 commentary records that Ibn Abbas and Mujahid proposed specific identifications including Thurayya (the Pleiades) or Saturn (Zuhal). Imam al-Tabari, after surveying these opinions, leaned toward the general interpretation — that every star is a 'thaqib' piercing the darkness — since the theological symbolic meaning matters more than identifying one specific celestial object.

questions.question: What was the majority view among early Companion commentators regarding the terms 'sulb' and 'tara'ib' in verse 7, as recorded by al-Tabari and supported by Ibn Kathir?
options: A. Both terms refer exclusively to female anatomy
B. 'Sulb' refers to the man's lumbar spine region and 'tara'ib' to the woman's chest area, together describing the combined origins of new human life from both parents
C. Both terms are purely metaphorical with no anatomical meaning
D. 'Sulb' and 'tara'ib' both refer to the male backbone alone
questions.explanation: The layer 2 tafsir records that Ibn Abbas explained 'sulb' as the region of the man and 'tara'ib' as the region of the woman. Al-Shanqiti in Adwa al-Bayan reconciled the Companion opinions by arguing the verse describes the combined fluid of both parents, consistent with the hadith in Sahih Muslim where the Prophet explained that a child is formed from the fluid of both.

questions.question: True or false: the rhetorical doubling in verse 17 ('fa-mahhil... amhilhum') is identified by scholars as an intensification device meaning the Prophet is being told emphatically to hold back and allow the divine plan to unfold.
questions.explanation: The layer 2 tafsir of verse 17 explains that the doubling of 'fa-mahhil' and 'amhilhum' is the device known as 'al-ta'kid bil-muradif' (intensification through a synonymous term). Al-Tabari records that the Companions understood this emphatic repetition as a declaration that the disbelievers' time was already nearly finished and the verse was revealed to comfort the Prophet during the Meccan period.

questions.question: Wahbah al-Zuhayli's commentary on the oath by 'the sky that returns' (verse 11) places it within which argumentative strategy?
options: A. Al-tawatur: establishing eschatological certainty through mass-transmitted hadith chains
B. Istidlal bil-makhlugat: arguing from the observable precision of the rain cycle to the Creator's power, using it as proof that the promised resurrection is equally certain
C. Al-ijaz al-adabi: demonstrating the Quran's literary inimitability through the beauty of nature imagery alone
D. Al-naskh: showing that earlier revelations about patience are abrogated by this surah's cosmic oaths
questions.explanation: The layer 3 tafsir records that Wahbah al-Zuhayli in al-Tafsir al-Munir highlights the verse's cosmological grandeur as proof of divine omnipotence within the strategy of istidlal bil-makhlugat — arguing from creation to Creator. The reliable return of rain demonstrates that the promised return of resurrection is equally certain, both stemming from the same divine power.

questions.question: What does Ibn Uthaymeen say verse 14 ('it is not jest') obligates the believer to do in practical terms?
options: A. To memorize the entire Quran before engaging with any of its meanings
B. To adopt a posture of ta'dhim (reverence) and ihtiraam (respect) toward the Quran in all circumstances, approaching it with seriousness rather than casualness
C. To refrain from reciting the Quran in public settings where non-Muslims are present
D. To limit Quranic study exclusively to scholars and avoid lay interpretation
questions.explanation: The layer 3 commentary records that Ibn Uthaymeen in his tafsir of Juz' Amma emphasizes that verse 14 obliges the believer to a posture of ta'dhim (reverence) and ihtiraam (respect) toward the Quran in all circumstances. The verse's categorical negation of 'hazl' (jest and frivolity) means that only serious, reverential engagement is appropriate for a text of such ultimate gravity.
